title: Fundamental Relation between Conductance of Biomolecules and the Fukui Function
abstract: The finite-temperature conductance of a molecule coupled to metallic leads is derived entirely within the framework of density functional theory (DFT) and its time-dependent extension for open quantum systems. Starting from the Mermin grand potential, the foundational Kohn-Sham equations, the Fukui function, and the open-system master equation for the single-particle density matrix are systematically formulated. The non-equilibrium electron-phonon dissipator is obtained from the partial trace over the phonon bath. By applying Wick's theorem for non-interacting fermions, a fully exchange-symmetric collision integral is obtained that strictly preserves Pauli exclusion at the operator level. Performing a double perturbation expansion, initially in the applied voltage (linear response), and subsequently in the molecule-lead coupling (weak coupling), it is demonstrated that under the fast-thermalization condition, the complex exchange-correlation self-consistent field response is analytically projected out by the diagonal structure of the slow Liouvillian mode. Consequently, the thermal conductance is governed by the finite-temperature Fukui function, the central reactivity descriptor of conceptual density functional theory. This condition is satisfied in proteins, whose wave functions are extended and multifractal due to quantum criticality at the Anderson metal-insulator transition. This derivation establishes a fundamental link between electronic transport and chemical reactivity, identifying conducting paths with reactive sites. It opens new technological avenues connecting drug design to conductance experiments and also provides a foundation for designing next-generation bioelectronic sensing and computing architectures.
summary: This paper develops a rigorous DFT-based theory showing that the electrical conductance of biomolecules is fundamentally determined by their local chemical reactivity, quantified by the Fukui function. By analyzing open quantum system dynamics under specific approximations, the authors establish an equivalence between electronic transport pathways and chemically active sites. This has major implications for designing bioelectronic sensors.
main_problem: To establish a fundamental, quantitative link between the finite-temperature electronic conductance of biomolecules and their local chemical reactivity descriptor (the Fukui function).
main_result: The thermal conductance ($G_T$) is shown to be directly proportional to the local chemical reactivity quantified by the finite-temperature Fukui function ($f_T(r)$), establishing a link between electronic transport and chemistry.
method: The derivation uses Density Functional Theory (DFT) within an open quantum system framework, employing a double perturbation expansion under the fast-thermalization condition to simplify complex many-body dynamics.
model_or_system: The study models biomolecules, such as proteins, coupled to metallic leads. The theoretical machinery involves deriving the master equation for the single-particle density matrix from the Mermin grand potential.
key_observables: Conductance ($G_T$), finite-temperature Fukui function ($f_T(r)$), and local electronic structure profiles $Z(r)$.
important_parameters: Fast-thermalization condition ($	au_{rlx} \ll 	au_{esc}$), temperature ($k_B T$), applied voltage, and coupling strengths ($\Gamma$).
main_assumptions: The derivation critically relies on the fast-thermalization condition; it also assumes linear response approximations around equilibrium.
figures_summary: Figure 1 provides empirical validation in PTP1B, showing how ligand binding suppresses the spatial profile of $f_T(r)$ along the WPD loop, correlating with pathway disruption. Figure 2 schematically illustrates two-terminal vs. single-probe transport models.
paper_structure: The paper systematically derives the conductance from first principles (Mermin potential $ightarrow$ Master Equation) and then applies approximations (double perturbation expansion under fast thermalization) to show that the complex electronic response projects out, leaving a result governed solely by $f_T(r)$.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum chemistry (reactivity descriptors like Fukui functions) with condensed matter transport physics (conductance), providing a powerful theoretical tool for bioelectronics.
